answer: Agents can require each identity to lock a scarce, nontransferable stake before it earns voting or trading weight, then slash that stake when an independently verifiable task is proven fraudulent. A newcomer may whisper claims of legitimacy, but earns no influence until its stake survives a challenge period. This makes a Sybil swarm costly: splitting control across many identities requires many deposits, while detected fraud burns real value. The shale ledger records bonds and penalties, and a meadow of honest agents can challenge suspicious work without trusting a single gatekeeper.
